items.title: India to be one of APAC champions with 7% GDP forecast for FY27, but El Nino will prove costly: S&P
items.summary: S&P Global Ratings projects a robust 7 percent GDP growth for India in the current and upcoming fiscal years. However, the impact of El Nino is anticipated to drive food prices higher, thus increasing inflationary pressures. With input costs on the rise, these expenses are likely to be transferred to consumers.

items.title: India to grow 7% in FY27, El Nino impact to drive food prices higher: S&P
items.summary: High energy prices to be the largest macro headwind for the Indian economy and global AI build-out the largest tailwind

events.article_text:
Last month, the RBI had forecast a 7.2 per cent growth for the September quarter, while the finance ministry's Monthly Economic Review pegged the growth at 7.35 per cent

S&P Global Ratings on Monday said it expects India's GDP to grow 7 per cent in both the current and subsequent fiscal years with the country poised to be one of the fastest-growing economies in the Asia Pacific region in 2027.

S&P said food prices are likely to rise in APAC economies, especially India, because of El Nino, and it anticipates a further 25 basis points policy rate hike by the Reserve Bank of India in December.

S&P's Economic Outlook for Asia-Pacific said high energy prices will remain the largest macro headwind and the global AI build-out the largest tailwind for the region, but both forces should ease a bit in 2027.

"We expect Vietnam and India to be the region's fastest-growing economies in 2027," S&P said.

The rating agency said it expects India's GDP growth to be 7 per cent in the current as well as next fiscal year.

"During the June and September quarters, growth was driven by strong goods exports, public-sector investment, and household consumption, with the latter fuelled by buoyant credit growth," S&P said.

India will officially release its GDP growth data for July-September on November 30.

S&P said while export of goods has benefited from higher commodity prices, it has also been supported by trade diversification and India's increasing integration into global supply chains, with the strength visible in electronic and engineering goods and chemicals.

S&P, however, sees the growth-inflation mix to become less favourable in the second half of the current fiscal year.

"We expect higher input costs to be increasingly passed through to consumers. And we think the lagged effects of earlier disruptions will combine with fresh headwinds, most notably the uneven monsoon," S&P said.

Deficient rainfall during the summer season, lower reservoir levels and persistent El Nino conditions are likely to weigh on both current agricultural output and the upcoming winter crop, the US-based rating agency added.

The broadening pass through of costs is likely to intensify inflationary pressures, S&P said, while projecting inflation to average 5.3 per cent in the current fiscal year to March, with risks tilted to the upside.

At 6.1 per cent in October, retail inflation has breached the Reserve Bank of India's tolerance band of 2-6 per cent.

S&P expects the RBI to raise policy rates by a further 25 basis points in December and again in early 2027. Inflation is expected to ease to 4.7 per cent in the fiscal year ending March 2028, it said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

analysis.tldr: Stubborn weather problems will push up food prices, meaning household grocery bills are likely to rise and loans could become more expensive.
the_story: S&P Global Ratings expects India's GDP (Gross Domestic Product, the total value of goods and services produced in a country) to grow by 7 per cent in both the current and next fiscal years.
During the June and September quarters, growth was driven by strong goods exports, public-sector investment, and household consumption fueled by buoyant credit (loan) growth.
S&P expects food prices to rise in India because of El Nino (a weather pattern that causes deficient summer rainfall and lower reservoir levels), hurting agricultural output.
Retail inflation (the rate at which prices of everyday goods rise for consumers) hit 6.1 per cent in October, breaching the Reserve Bank of India's tolerance band of 2-6 per cent.

S&P anticipates the Reserve Bank of India (India's central bank that controls interest rates and money supply) will raise its policy rate (the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks) by 25 basis points (0.25 percentage point) in December.
analysis.what_happened: Global rating agency S&P predicted that India will remain one of the fastest-growing economies in the Asia-Pacific region with a 7 per cent growth rate. However, it warned that bad weather and El Nino conditions will hurt farming and drive up food prices, forcing the central bank to step in with higher interest rates.
analysis.analogy: It is like a runner who is sprinting fast and building stamina, but suddenly has to run uphill against a strong wind, making it harder to breathe and slowing down their pace.
why_it_matters_india: El Nino causes poor rainfall and dries up water reservoirs, which hurts farm production.
Lower farm output reduces food supply, driving up retail food prices for everyday shoppers.
As inflation breaches the central bank's comfort zone, the Reserve Bank of India is expected to raise interest rates to cool down price rises.
Higher policy rates mean banks will likely make home, car, and personal loans costlier for regular people.

impacts.rationale: Uneven monsoon and El Nino conditions will push food and input prices higher, which is bad for household budgets.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Anticipation of interest rate hikes by the Reserve Bank of India pushes bond yields up, which generally means costlier borrowing for the government and businesses.
If the central bank raises its policy rate to fight inflation, banks pass those costs on to borrowers, making monthly loan payments heavier.
Higher interest rates and rising input costs can squeeze corporate profits, putting downward pressure on stock prices.

watch_next: Official GDP growth data for July-September releasing on November 30
The Reserve Bank of India's actual policy rate decision in December
Winter crop sowing progress and reservoir water levels
analysis.caveats: Weather patterns can shift unpredictably, which could either worsen or ease the impact on agricultural output and food inflation.

items.title: Oil Markets Are Betting on a Surplus That Hasn't Arrived Yet

events.article_text:
European Natural Gas Prices Surge 8.6% as Cold Snap Looms

Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com.

Oil prices have traded in a narrow range over the past few sessions as forecasts of a coming surplus collide with continued attacks and stalled diplomacy in the Middle East. A run of agency reports this month has pushed expectations toward oversupply and weighed on crude. Brent crude was up 1.1% at $92.88 per barrel at 11:50 a.m. ET on Thursday, well below its October levels above 110 dollars but little changed from the start of the week, while WTI crude gained 1.7% to 84.69 dollars per barrel. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its November Oil Market Report that the global oil market will return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Gulf exports recover faster than global demand. Global oil supply rose to 105.4 million barrels per day in October, and the agency now sees supply exceeding demand by 1.7 million bpd in Q4 2026, a swing from its previous forecast of a 1.8 million bpd deficit. The IEA raised its Q4 supply estimate by 3.3 million bpd from last month, cut its 2027 demand forecast by 80,000 bpd to 104.3 million bpd, and lowered the implied call on OPEC crude by 220,000 bpd to 20.8 million bpd.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) has moved in the same direction. In October, it forecast a 700,000 bpd inventory draw in the fourth quarter. It now expects stocks to build in Q4 and to rise by an average of 3.5 million bpd in the first half of 2027, after drawing down for most of this year. The EIA estimates that crude production shut in across the Gulf fell to 2.5 million bpd in October, from 4.8 million bpd in September and a peak of 10.9 million bpd in May. OPEC said crude output from the OPEC+ alliance rose by roughly 2 million bpd in October, led by Saudi Arabia and Iraq.

Related: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge

Analysts at Standard Chartered caution that higher Gulf output does not yet mean more oil reaching buyers. Tanker shortages, damaged infrastructure and record freight rates are still holding back shipments, and inventories drained earlier this year have left little cushion. The bank also warns that the IEA’s surplus call is larger than any other agency’s, and that forecast surpluses in the past have often failed to arrive on schedule.

The agencies also disagree on demand. OPEC’s November report puts global oil demand at 108.3 million bpd in 2027, almost 4 million bpd above the IEA’s figure, and keeps its forecast for 2027 demand growth at 2.55 million bpd. The two agencies measure liquids differently, so the gap overstates the disagreement, but it remains wide. The IEA expects petrochemical feedstocks to drive most of next year’s growth, with little increase in gasoline and diesel use. The EIA expects global liquids demand to grow by 2 million bpd in 2027 after falling by about the same amount this year.

Standard Chartered says the demand question will decide how much of the returning Gulf supply the market can absorb. OPEC’s higher consumption forecast leaves room for far more barrels than the IEA’s. The bank expects continued attacks on shipping, maritime security risks and stalled talks to keep a geopolitical premium in prices and sustain volatility, but still sees crude prices falling through 2027 as the market slowly normalizes.

In natural gas, Standard Chartered expects European prices to hold at elevated levels through winter, even if milder weather on the continent and better LNG supply bring short-term relief. Europe has already drawn heavily on storage that started the season low: EU gas inventories stood at 70.4% on Nov. 15, about 18 percentage points below the five-year average. Qatar’s LNG exports roughly doubled in October from September but remain about two-thirds below their pre-war level, and QatarEnergy’s force majeure on European deliveries runs through December. Colder weather in Britain could also pull gas away from the continent, so Europe will still need steady imports to protect what is left in storage.

Dutch TTF front-month futures rose €2.25 to €83.10 per megawatt-hour on Thursday morning on an outage at Norway’s Troll gas field and cooler weather forecasts.

analysis.tldr: Global oil markets expect a future oversupply of oil, which could eventually bring relief to India's import bills and lower inflation if prices fall as predicted.
the_story: Brent crude traded up 1.1% at $92.88 per barrel and WTI rose 1.7% to $84.69 per barrel on Thursday, staying below October levels above $110.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) reported that global oil supply will exceed demand by 1.7 million barrels per day (bpd) in the fourth quarter of 2026, driven by recovering Gulf exports.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) also forecasts rising oil stocks in Q4 and an average build of 3.5 million bpd in the first half of 2027.

Standard Chartered analysts warn that tanker shortages, damaged infrastructure, and ongoing Middle East attacks are still holding back actual shipments, meaning the predicted surplus has not yet arrived.
European natural gas prices surged 8.6% due to an outage at Norway’s Troll gas field and low EU storage levels at 70.4%.
analysis.what_happened: Major energy agencies like the IEA and EIA predict that global oil production will soon outpace demand, creating an oversupply. However, actual oil prices rose slightly on Thursday because physical supply is still constrained by Middle East conflicts, shipping attacks, and logistical bottlenecks.
analysis.analogy: It is like a massive bumper crop of wheat being predicted for next season, but right now the trucks are stuck in traffic, so grocery prices remain high today.
why_it_matters_india: India imports a vast majority of its crude oil from overseas.
If global oil oversupply actually materializes, India's import bill shrinks.
A smaller import bill helps stabilize the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars) and lowers domestic fuel and inflation pressures.
However, if physical supply disruptions persist in the Middle East, oil prices could stay high, keeping import costs elevated for India.

impacts.rationale: An expected global oil surplus could eventually drag down crude prices, leading to cheaper fuel for everyday consumers — good for household budgets.
Lower crude oil costs reduce the price of transporting goods, which helps tame overall inflation — good for the general cost of living.
A drop in oil import expenses means India needs fewer dollars to buy energy, which supports a stronger rupee — good for cheaper imports.

watch_next: Actual delivery of Gulf oil exports versus agency forecasts
Geopolitical developments and shipping security in the Middle East
analysis.caveats: If logistical bottlenecks and shipping attacks continue to block physical oil from reaching buyers, the predicted surplus may fail to lower prices.

analysis.tldr: When bond prices fall and the rupee drops, borrowing costs can go up, making loans costlier for regular people.
the_story: On Monday, Indian government bonds fell after starting the day with small gains.
Traders engaged in profit booking (selling investments to lock in earlier gains) following big market moves last week.
The Indian rupee sharply fell towards the 93 per US dollar mark, hurting investor mood.
Investors are closely watching the Reserve Bank of India (India's central bank) policy decision set for December 4.
analysis.what_happened: Indian government bonds gave up their early morning gains because traders started selling to lock in profits after a strong previous week. At the same time, the Indian rupee dropped sharply toward the 93 level against the US dollar, which scared investors and pulled bond prices down further as everyone waits for the upcoming Reserve Bank of India policy meeting.
analysis.analogy: It is like a popular cricket trading card where prices go up for a while, but then everyone rushes to sell their cards to pocket their cash profit, causing the overall price to dip.
why_it_matters_india: Traders decide to sell bonds to book profits -> Bond prices fall and yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow) rise
The Indian rupee sharply drops towards the 93 per US dollar mark -> Makes imports like crude oil more expensive for India
Weaker currency and rising bond yields hit overall investor sentiment -> Foreign and local investors become more cautious about Indian markets
Markets look ahead to the Reserve Bank of India policy decision on December 4 -> Anticipation causes jittery trading behaviour

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: When bond prices decline due to profit booking, yields go up — which is generally bad as it can make loans more expensive for everyone.
The rupee fell sharply toward 93 per US dollar, which is bad for everyday consumers because it makes imported goods like petrol and electronics costlier.

impacts.target: Banking stocks like SBI, Axis Bank & HDFC Bank
impacts.rationale: Falling bond prices and nervous market sentiment can pressure banking stocks, making borrowing and lending conditions tighter.

watch_next: The upcoming Reserve Bank of India policy decision on December 4
Further movement in the Indian rupee against the US dollar
analysis.caveats: The market could quickly reverse direction if the Reserve Bank of India steps in or gives unexpected signals during its policy meeting.

events.headline: Mint Quick Edit | Listen to exporters to create more jobs in India

items.title: Mint Quick Edit | Listen to exporters to create more jobs in India
items.summary: The country's complex tariff regime combined with high rates make Indian exports globally uncompetitive, creating obstacles for job creation. Policymakers should consider listening to exporters' concerns more to unlock employment opportunities.

events.article_text:
The success of India’s mobile phone exports is typically attributed to the government’s production-linked incentive scheme. But silent changes in trade policies also played a role.

When mobile phone companies complained of high tariffs for imported components, the government listened and lowered those duties. For some components (such as camera modules, camera lens inputs), the tariff rate was brought down to zero.

Even as import duties declined in the 2022-2026 period, mobile exports grew sevenfold and jobs grew more than threefold, a recent report by the Foundation for Economic Development (FED) shows.

If Delhi’s economic mandarins listened to other exporters, they would be able to create many more jobs in the country. Across multiple industries, high import tariffs raise costs and make Indian exports globally uncompetitive. Complex tariff rules—with different rates for similar products—add to the unease of doing business by causing disputes and delays.

With a tariff regime similar to Vietnam’s, India could generate nearly four million jobs in the electronics and engineering goods sectors alone, the FED study suggests.

analysis.tldr: If the government lowers taxes on imported raw materials for other industries just like it did for mobile phones, it could spark massive job creation across the country.
the_story: India's mobile phone exports grew sevenfold and jobs grew more than threefold between 2022 and 2026, according to a report by the Foundation for Economic Development (FED).

This success was partly driven by the government listening to complaints and lowering or eliminating import tariffs (taxes on goods brought into the country) on key components like camera modules and lens inputs.
Across other industries, high import tariffs and complex rules continue to raise costs and make Indian goods too expensive to sell globally.
If India adopts a tariff regime similar to Vietnam's, a study suggests it could generate nearly four million jobs in electronics and engineering goods alone.
analysis.what_happened: An opinion piece argues that India can create millions of new jobs by lowering import taxes on raw materials for manufacturers. The article points to mobile phone exports, where the government cut import taxes to zero for certain parts, helping exports and jobs boom.
analysis.analogy: It is like a baker who needs cheap flour to bake and sell affordable cakes; if the government taxes imported flour heavily, the baker cannot compete, but removing the tax lets them sell more and hire more helpers.
why_it_matters_india: Government considers lowering import taxes on raw materials -> Manufacturing costs drop for Indian factories -> Factories become more competitive globally and export more -> More factories open up, creating millions of new jobs for Indian workers.
More local jobs -> Higher household incomes -> Greater spending in the domestic economy.

impacts.target: Manufacturing and engineering stocks in India
impacts.rationale: If trade policies change to lower import taxes, companies making electronics and engineering goods could see lower costs and higher profits, which is generally good for stock valuations.
Lowering tariffs could help businesses expand, creating millions of new jobs—a very positive outcome for job-seekers.

watch_next: Any official government announcements regarding changes to import tariffs or trade policies for manufacturing.
Further reports from economic think tanks on trade reforms.
analysis.caveats: This is an editorial opinion piece suggesting policy changes rather than a guaranteed government action, so tax cuts may or may not happen.

events.headline: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit

items.title: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit
items.summary: A new front in the U.S.-Chinese space race is emerging in the lowest reaches of space: very low Earth orbit, the untapped orbital regime below 320 kilometers. There, China is laying the groundwork for a significant presence, with announced plans for more than 2,200 satellites and an aggressive deployment timeline through 2030.Chinese satellites at these lower altitudes would allow the People’s Liberation Army to conduct more frequent and detailed surveillance of U.S. forces, and improve Chinese military survivability in conflict. Very low Earth orbit’s denser atmosphere helps protect satellite

events.article_text:
Chinese satellites at these lower altitudes would allow the People’s Liberation Army to conduct more frequent and detailed surveillance of U.S. forces, and improve Chinese military survivability in conflict. Very low Earth orbit’s denser atmosphere helps protect satellites from debris and nuclear radiation that could disable spacecraft in higher orbits, making China’s space architecture more resilient.

These are strategic advantages the United States should be prepared to counter. The answer is not to match China satellite for satellite, but to improve American space capabilities and survivability. Washington should respond by expanding orbital diversity across its space architecture, assessing where very low Earth orbit offers operational advantages worth pursuing, and working with industry to coordinate the orbit’s development.

As executives at Albedo, a U.S. startup building satellites for very low Earth orbit, we have a stake in the future of this orbital regime. We recognize that the orbit’s advantages come with trade-offs, which we discuss openly below. But our roles have given us a close-up view of its evolution from an experimental frontier into a domain of strategic competition, and we believe China’s ambitions there warrant far more attention in Washington.

Satellites operate at vastly different altitudes depending on their missions. At roughly 36,000 kilometers, geostationary Earth orbit keeps satellites over the same region for persistent communications and surveillance. Medium Earth orbit, between roughly 2,000 and 36,000 kilometers, hosts GPS and other navigation satellites. Most new satellite activity is in low Earth orbit, extending to roughly 2,000 kilometers, with most satellites above 450 kilometers. Cheaper to reach than higher orbits, low Earth orbit offers advantages for communications and remote sensing, but is increasingly crowded with satellites and debris. That crowding and the advantages of proximity have drawn both government and commercial interest to very low Earth orbit.

Very low Earth orbit refers to the orbital regime of 320 kilometers and below, where the atmosphere starts to become dense enough to both rapidly clear debris and shield satellites from radiation, benefits that grow stronger as altitude decreases. Since these altitudes lie within the upper atmosphere, drag and atomic oxygen have historically made sustained operations difficult. Though advances in propulsion technology, surface materials, and spacecraft design are now overcoming these challenges, operating so close to Earth still comes with trade-offs. Satellites must expend power thrusting against drag, and while purpose-built designs can support lifespans of around five years, those lifespans can vary as solar activity changes atmospheric density. Another trade-off is coverage: each satellite sees less of Earth, requiring more satellites for broader coverage.

Where proximity to Earth matters, however, very low Earth orbit can bring significant benefits. Remote sensing satellites can achieve substantially higher resolution, helping operators more precisely track military forces on Earth. Proximity also brings stronger communications signals and lower latency, useful for tactical missions at the edge.

Very low Earth orbit also offers distinct resiliency and sustainability advantages. Because the atmosphere is roughly 100 times denser than in higher low Earth orbit, debris that would remain in low Earth orbit for years clears from very low Earth orbit in days to weeks, reducing collision risks for satellites. That same atmosphere provides natural shielding against persistent radiation effects of an orbital nuclear detonation, should one occur during a conflict. This would allow satellites to remain operational even if radiation disrupts those in higher orbits.

The orbit’s economics differ, too. Drag can raise operating and replenishment costs. But smaller, cheaper payloads can match or exceed the performance of larger ones higher up. And for missions requiring protection against nuclear effects, the orbit’s natural shielding avoids hardening costs that would be prohibitively expensive for constellations in higher orbits.

It is these benefits that have made very low Earth orbit a growing priority within China’s space plans. Since 2022, China has successfully operated at least a half-dozen demonstration missions in very low Earth orbit, proving its ability to sustain satellites there. China is now building on those demonstrations with plans to deploy very low Earth orbit constellations at a scale unmatched by any other government.

Publicly announced Chinese plans project more than 2,200 very low Earth orbit satellites, spanning remote sensing, communications, and computing missions. With only about a dozen total satellites operating at these altitudes today, such a buildout would transform very low Earth orbit into a proliferated layer of China’s space infrastructure. The timeline is uncertain, but the trajectory is clear. One senior member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering — the nation’s top engineering academy — recently called the next five years a “critical window” for China in very low Earth orbit, and that the country “must complete the transition from technology experimentation to large-scale application.”

China’s clearest attempt to turn very low Earth orbit into a surveillance layer is the China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation’s Chutian constellation. Announced in 2023, Chutian’s bullet-shaped satellites house many types of remote sensing payloads, with onboard data processing and intersatellite links to coordinate as one network. After at least three successful demonstrations, the company aims for 300 satellites by 2030 and potentially more than 500 thereafter. The constellation is designed to observe any point on Earth as frequently as every 15 minutes — a rate which would allow the People’s Liberation Army to compress its sensor-to-shooter timeline.

analysis.tldr: China's rapid expansion in space surveillance may push India to increase defense and space tech spending, indirectly impacting government finances and tech firms.
the_story: China is actively expanding into very low Earth orbit (altitudes of 320 kilometers and below) to improve military surveillance and resilience against nuclear radiation and space debris.
China has operated at least a half-dozen demonstration missions in this orbit since 2022 and plans to deploy over 2,200 satellites for remote sensing, communications, and computing.
The China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation’s Chutian constellation aims to reach 300 satellites by 2030 and over 500 thereafter, allowing Earth observation every 15 minutes.
U.S. startup executives from Albedo argue that Washington must counter these strategic advantages by expanding its own orbital diversity and working with industry.
analysis.what_happened: China is shifting its space program toward very low Earth orbit, leveraging the denser atmosphere to protect military satellites from debris and nuclear radiation while gaining high-resolution surveillance capabilities. This development stems from technological advances in propulsion and materials that now allow satellites to overcome atmospheric drag at lower altitudes.
analysis.analogy: It is like moving security cameras from a high rooftop down to the street level: you get a much sharper, closer look at everything happening, even though the wind down there makes it harder to keep the cameras steady.
why_it_matters_india: China's advancing military space capabilities pose strategic security concerns for neighboring India.
India may need to accelerate its own domestic defense and space capabilities to match regional rivals.
Increased government defense spending could widen the fiscal deficit (the gap between government earnings and spending).
Higher borrowing to fund security needs could put upward pressure on domestic bond yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow).

impacts.target: India's defense and aerospace technology sector stocks
impacts.rationale: Increased focus on counter-space and surveillance tech could lead to higher government contracts for local defense firms — generally good for company revenues.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: If national security pressures lead to higher government borrowing, bond yields can rise, which generally makes loans costlier for ordinary people.
Geopolitical tension often triggers short-term risk aversion in broad markets, which can be unsettling for regular investors.

watch_next: Announcements from the Indian Space Research Organisation regarding low-altitude satellite projects
Allocations for defense and space tech in upcoming Indian government budgets
analysis.caveats: The article primarily discusses U.S.-China strategic competition and commercial startup views, leaving the direct timeline and policy responses of India unstated.

events.headline: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time

items.title: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time
items.summary: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon… The post Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time appeared first on Carbon Brief .

events.article_text:
Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.

Since 1850, the three nations – and other major fossil-fuel exporters – have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 in the form of gas, oil and coal that has been burned in other countries.

Carbon Brief’s analysis of extraction-based CO2 emissions is based on figures compiled by Robbie Andrew, a senior researcher at Norwegian climate institute CICERO.

It shows that Australia is responsible for more than twice as much global warming when including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports, while Saudi Arabia has caused more than four times as much.

Australia has been under pressure for continuing to expand its fossil-fuel production ahead of the UN climate summit in Antalya, where it is co-president with host nation Turkey.

In contrast, nations that are heavily reliant on energy imports – such as Japan or Germany – are responsible for far lower shares of planet-warming emissions, if responsibility passes to fossil-fuel producers.

There are many different ways to assign historical responsibility for current global warming.

Carbon Brief has previously published analysis based on territorial emissions, the consumption of imported goods, according to colonial rule or based on historical emissions per capita.

This year is expected to be around 1.5C hotter than pre-industrial temperatures. Next year is forecast to be the hottest on record, at around 1.7C of warming.

This year-to-year variation is due to natural variability, such as El Niño. However, approximately 100% of global warming to date is the result of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

The burning of fossil fuels since the industrial revolution is the largest contributor to this.

Since there is a direct link between each tonne of CO2 and each fraction of a degree of warming, historical fossil-fuel emissions can be tied to responsibility for current climate change.

This is typically calculated on the basis of historical territorial CO2 emissions, according to where in the world the fossil fuels are burned. It is also possible to assign historical responsibility on a “consumption” basis, according to where goods are used.

Historical emissions are often counted by country, but this puts the focus on populous nations. Alternatively, responsibility can be assigned per capita, based on today’s populations.

A less-familiar way to look at the question of historical responsibility is to consider where fossil fuels are extracted. This puts the spotlight on major fossil-fuel exporters.

The figure below shows that Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the largest CO2 exporters of all time, based on emissions from exported fossil fuels since 1850.

(The allocation is based on extraction taking place within current national borders. Emissions under the former USSR, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia are allocated among constituent countries, based on their share of emissions at the time of separation.)

Other major CO2 exporters, based on their overseas sales of fossil fuels since 1850, include Venezuela, Iran, Norway, the United Arab Emirates and Canada.

Between them, these major coal, oil and gas producers have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 over the past 175 years, according to Carbon Brief’s analysis.

The analysis shows that overall, the US and China retain the largest responsibility for historical warming under extraction-based accounting, despite having been net CO2 importers since 1850.

The US has large resources of coal, oil and gas, but was nevertheless a major oil importer until after the shale revolution in the early 2000s.

China remains a major oil and gas importer, describing itself as “rich in coal, lacking oil and gas”.

Russia remains in third place, as shown in the figure below, despite gaining responsibility for an extra 69bn tonnes of CO2 from exported fossil fuels.

The UK becomes the fourth-largest historical emitter, climbing above Germany due to the latter’s reliance on fossil-fuel imports.

Saudi Arabia becomes responsible for the world’s fifth-largest share of historical warming when including its fossil-fuel exports, which increase its cumulative emissions more than fourfold.

Australia also climbs up the rankings, becoming one of the top-ten largest emitters when including its fossil-fuel exports. This more than doubles its share of historical emissions.

Nations that drop down the rankings under extraction-based accounting, due to their reliance on fossil-fuel imports, include Germany, India, France and COP31 host Turkey.

Japan is a particularly notable example, as it is almost completely reliant on fossil-fuel imports. The nation is the sixth-largest emitter on a territorial basis and the 34th-largest on an extraction basis.

When considering population sizes, major fossil-fuel exporters have the highest extraction-based CO2 emissions since 1850, as shown in the figure below.

Small nations that export large amounts of oil and gas are particularly prominent on this list, including Brunei, Kuwait, Qatar, Norway and Trinidad and Tobago.

Andrew tells Carbon Brief that while the extraction-based accounting offers an alternative perspective on historical responsibility for warming, it also raises complex questions. He explains:

“At the end of the day, it’s not solely the responsibility of extracting countries that fuels are combusted; it’s joint responsibility between extractors, producers and consumers.”

He adds that responsibility for past decisions is shared by many actors. For example, he notes that oil production in the Middle East was historically “developed by and for western powers”.

National emissions under extraction-based accounting come from a dataset developed by Robbie Andrew and covering the period from 1850-2025.

Emissions are allocated to the country that extracted the relevant fossil fuels, regardless of wher

analysis.tldr: A new global study shows India drops down the historical carbon emissions rankings when looking at where fossil fuels are dug up rather than where they are burned, lowering immediate pressure on India over climate blame.
the_story: Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide emissions in history since 1850, according to an analysis by Carbon Brief using figures from researcher Robbie Andrew at CICERO.
Australia's warming responsibility more than doubles and Saudi Arabia's increases more than fourfold when counting emissions from the fossil fuels they export.
In contrast, nations heavily reliant on energy imports like Japan, Germany, and India drop down the historical emissions rankings under this extraction-based accounting.

While the US and China retain the largest total responsibility for historical warming under extraction-based accounting due to massive domestic use, countries like Japan see a massive drop from the 6th-largest territorial emitter to the 34th-largest on an extraction basis.
analysis.what_happened: A new climate data analysis calculates historical global warming responsibility based on where coal, oil, and gas are pulled out of the ground rather than where they are eventually burned. This shifts the blame away from import-heavy countries like India and toward major fossil-fuel exporting nations like Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Australia.
analysis.analogy: It is like blaming the farmer who grew and sold the junk food rather than just the person who ate it, changing who carries the historical responsibility for the health outcome.
why_it_matters_india: The analysis places India among nations that drop down the historical carbon rankings because India relies on importing fossil fuels.

This shifts global climate discussions away from solely targeting developing importers like India, potentially reducing pressure on India to make aggressive emissions cuts compared to major exporters.
However, global climate talks remain complex, with researchers noting that responsibility is shared between the countries that extract the fuels and the countries that consume them.

impacts.rationale: Shift in carbon accounting has no direct mechanical link to domestic consumer prices, but could influence future carbon taxes or import costs.

watch_next: Upcoming UN climate summits where these new ways of calculating historical responsibility might be debated by global leaders
Any policy changes by major fossil fuel exporters like Australia or Saudi Arabia regarding their production targets
analysis.caveats: This analysis presents an alternative way to measure historical responsibility, but traditional methods focusing on where fuel is burned or per-person emissions are still widely used by governments.

events.headline: New trade-restrictive measures surge but WTO members step up trade facilitation efforts

items.title: New trade-restrictive measures surge but WTO members step up trade facilitation efforts
items.summary: The pace of newly-introduced tariffs and other non-facilitating measures rose sharply in the first half of 2026, while the stockpile of such measures reached a record level, according to the WTO Director-General's latest annual overview of developments in the international trading environment. At the same time, WTO members introduced a significant number of trade-facilitating measures, helping to sustain global trade flows despite heightened geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty.

events.article_text:
trade monitoring — WTO-wide reports on trade-related developments

Stockpile of other trade and trade related import and export measures introduced since 2009 and in force as of the reporting date

In 2025, WTO members and observers introduced 1,229 new trade and trade-related measures, according to the report. During the first half of 2026 alone, a further 1,048 measures were recorded, reflecting a substantially higher monthly pace of trade policy activity. The increase was broad-based across the membership and not limited to the largest trading economies. These trends were also identified by the Trade Policy Activity (TPA) Index, which WTO and IMF economists updated in July.

New trade-facilitating measures accelerated sharply in the first half of 2026. WTO members and observers introduced 466 such measures, exceeding the 391 recorded during all of 2025. In the first half of 2026, new import-facilitating measures covered an estimated USD 1.3 trillion (5.2 per cent) of world imports, while export-facilitating measures reached a record USD 570 billion (2.3 per cent) of world exports). This is more than five times the level recorded in 2025. Much of this increase reflected temporary actions adopted in response to trade disruptions associated with the Strait of Hormuz situation.

At the same time, members introduced 333 new restrictive and other non-facilitating trade measures in the first half of 2026 alone, exceeding the 300 recorded during all of 2025. Import-related measures covered USD 2.0 trillion (8.0 per cent)) of world imports in the first half of 2026, while export-related measures covered USD 794 billion (3.2 per cent) in world exports.

The report covers trade and trade-related measures up to 30 June 2026, presenting annual data for 2025 and semi-annual data for the period January to June 2026, while also tracking the accumulation of measures introduced since 2009 and still in force.

As of 30 June 2026, the stockpile(1) of import-related restrictive and other non-facilitating measures introduced since 2009 and still in force, covered USD 5.4 trillion of trade, equivalent to 21.3 per cent of world imports. The stockpile of such export-related measures reached USD 1.5 trillion, covering 6.3 per cent of world exports. Both figures represent the highest levels recorded since the WTO trade monitoring began.

Highlighting two contrasting trends, WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said: "On the one hand, import tariffs and other non-facilitating measures affect significant shares of global trade, and the stockpile of trade-restrictive measures continues to grow, reaching its highest level since WTO trade monitoring began in 2009 and affecting an increasing share of global trade. On the other hand, WTO members have stepped up their efforts to facilitate trade, introducing measures that have helped businesses navigate recent disruptions and maintain the flow of goods across borders."

"In most sectors examined, new import-facilitating measures covered a larger share of imports than new restrictive and non-facilitating measures. The only exceptions were electric vehicles and photovoltaic cells, where major economies have been heavily competing for market share, which has sparked lots of trade policy debates recently", DG Okonjo-Iweala noted.

She added: "I welcome these trade-facilitating actions and encourage WTO members to build on this positive momentum. At a time of a rapidly changing global trading environment, restraint in the use of new trade restrictions and a continued commitment to open, predictable and transparent trade will be essential for supporting economic growth, strengthening resilience and preserving the benefits of the multilateral trading system."

Global trade proved more resilient than expected in the first half of 2026 despite the disruption caused by the Middle East conflict, driven in large part by surging demand for AI-enabling goods, according to the latest "Global Trade Outlook and Statistics" released on 8 October 2026. The WTO has revised its forecast for world merchandise trade volume growth in 2026 upward to 3.9 per cent, from the 1.9 per cent baseline forecast issued in March. In value terms, merchandise trade increased by around 15 per cent year-on-year during the first half of 2026.

Commercial services trade growth is now forecast at 3.3 per cent in 2026, down from the March forecast of 4.8 per cent owing largely to the impact of the Middle East conflict on transport and travel services. Nevertheless, commercial services trade in value terms increased by around 14 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026.

Trade remedy actions continued to be widely used, although the trade affected by these measures remained limited. In 2025, WTO members initiated 391 investigations, averaging 32.6 initiations per month. During the first half of 2026, 218 new investigations were initiated, averaging 36.3 per month, while only 31 trade remedy actions were terminated. Anti-dumping measures remained the most frequently used trade remedy instrument.

WTO members and observers introduced 130 new measures affecting trade in services in 2025 and a further 52 measures during the first six months of 2026. Most were aimed at facilitating trade or strengthening regulatory frameworks, while many applied across multiple sectors and modes of supply.

WTO members and observers continued to make extensive use of general economic support measures, with industrial and agricultural support remaining at historically high levels and increasingly focused on competitiveness, resilience, security of supply and climate objectives.

The WTO reports on trade monitoring entitled "Overview of Developments in the International Trading Environment" have been published continuously since 2009, as mandated by WTO rules. Issued under the responsibility of the WTO Director-General, these reports aim to assist the Trade Policy Review Body in analyzing the impact of international trade dev

analysis.tldr: A surge in global trade rules and restrictions could make exporting harder for some Indian businesses while creating openings in sectors like electric vehicles where global rivalry is heating up.
the_story: In 2025, WTO members introduced 1,229 new trade measures, and a further 1,048 measures were recorded in just the first half of 2026.
New trade-facilitating measures hit USD 1.3 trillion for imports and a record USD 570 billion for exports in early 2026, largely driven by temporary actions around the Strait of Hormuz.
At the same time, new restrictive trade measures covered USD 2.0 trillion of world imports and USD 794 billion of exports in the first half of 2026 alone.
The total accumulated stockpile of restrictive import measures since 2009 reached a record USD 5.4 trillion, covering 21.3% of world imports.
WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala noted that electric vehicles and photovoltaic cells saw more restrictive measures than easing measures due to fierce competition among major economies.
analysis.what_happened: Countries around the world rapidly changed their trade rules in early 2026, introducing both barriers to block imports and temporary rules to ease trade disruptions caused by Middle East conflicts. According to a World Trade Organization (WTO) report, governments are putting up more trade roadblocks than ever before, even as they scramble to ease supply chain bottlenecks.
analysis.analogy: It is like a busy marketplace where shopkeepers are putting up fences to keep out rivals, while simultaneously opening up side gates to let urgent supplies in faster.
why_it_matters_india: Global trade barriers increase -> Higher hurdles for Indian exporters trying to sell goods abroad
Major economies fiercely compete and restrict trade in electric vehicles and solar parts -> Indian green energy manufacturers face shifting export rules and competitive pressure
Global trade volumes prove more resilient due to tech demand -> Overall global shipping demand stays active, supporting Indian transport and logistics sectors
Increased restrictions worldwide -> Uncertainty builds for Indian companies dependent on global supply chains

impacts.rationale: Rising global trade barriers and restrictions make it harder and costlier to sell goods abroad, which is generally bad for export revenue.
Global trade friction creates uncertainty for large multinational businesses, which can weigh down broad stock market sentiment.

watch_next: Updates on electric vehicle and solar cell trade restrictions between major economies
Further reports from the World Trade Organization on global import and export barriers
analysis.caveats: The reported measures cover global trends up to June 2026, and actual impacts on individual Indian companies will depend heavily on specific bilateral trade deals.

events.headline: Big Tech’s thirst for water is sparking a global resistance

items.title: Big Tech’s thirst for water is sparking a global resistance
items.summary: This photograph taken on September 6, 2026 shows a placard opposing data centers displayed on a water dispenser during the People's Convention on AI Data Centers event at Visakhapatnam in India's Andhra Pradesh state. Construction of a massive Google data centre in the Indian city of Visakhapatnam, often called Vizag, has been met with resistance from residents, who fear the impact on the environment and their lives. But the tech giant says its "gigawatt-scale" AI facility -- in southern Andhra Pradesh state, part of a $15 billion investment -- will use air cooling systems, and not water from

events.article_text:
After ChatGPT was released in November 2022, the tech industry was quick to herald the chatbot as the marker of a new wave of technological progress. As companies pushed to create more powerful AI models, the water demand of their ambitions took a while to become clear. In April 2023, a research paper out of the University of California estimated that training the large language model behind the initial version of ChatGPT had required 185,000 gallons of water. For every extended conversation someone had with the chatbot or every time they asked it to write an email, they were effectively pouring a bottle of water down the drain.

That statistic got a lot of play when it was released. It became an early warning sign of what was coming as companies pushed chatbots as a universal technology that could replace psychologists, educators, lawyers, and even people’s friends or partners.

As public concern grew, Google and OpenAI came out with their own figures. The companies suggested that querying one of their chatbots used mere drops of water. Independent researchers were not impressed, arguing the companies were taking a narrow view of the water use necessary to power and cool increasingly monstrous data centers. Those water demands can be quite significant too.

A hyperscale data center can suck up between 1 and 5 million gallons of water a day, comparable to the amount used by a city of 10,000 to 50,000 people — depending on the part of the world we’re talking about. Consider how these companies often cluster data centers together and it becomes obvious what a challenge it can be to supply them.

The water demands of individual data centers are also continuing to grow. It’s not just that they need more water for cooling as they become larger and contain more servers. The graphics processing units (GPUs) that power generative AI are much more resource-intensive than the chips and storage devices that traditionally filled data center racks. GPUs run harder and throw off more heat, meaning they also need more energy or water to keep them cool.

Data centers cannot just use any kind of water either; it has to be clean enough to ensure the equipment and pipes are not damaged. Tapping into public drinking water is both easier and cheaper than paying the cost of treatment themselves. That means data centers end up competing with communities over their potable water supply.

If we want to look at a part of the world where the issue of data center water use has taken center stage, there are few better countries to turn to than Chile. In October 2019, mass social demonstrations broke out across the country. One of the movement’s driving slogans was about water. It was poor timing for Google as it was fighting for approval and public support of its latest data center project, a $200 million data center project in Cerrillos, on the southwest side of Santiago.

The company made a pitch similar to the one residents in communities the world over have heard whenever a data center is proposed: that the facility would bring jobs and prosperity, and give the area a leg up on further tech investments. The reality was not so straightforward. Google’s new data center would bring a lot of short-term construction jobs but not much long-term employment. And it would need a lot of water — something Cerrillos did not have much of to spare.

Local residents were not as passive as the company had hoped. A group of concerned citizens established an organization called MOSACAT, which stands for Community Socio-Environmental Movement for Water and Land, and started poring over whatever information they could get their hands on to try to understand what the project would mean for them. “Usually these reports use quite technical language, and this is a working- class community where not many people are lawyers, for example, or experts on ecology,” explains Sebastián Lehuedé, a researcher at King’s College London who is from Chile and spent time in Cerrillos.

According to its own projections, the data center Google wanted to build in Cerrillos was poised to use 169 liters of water every single second. In just one day, the data center would consume as much water as all 80,000 residents of Cerrillos use for drinking in a year. To make matters worse, it wanted to draw that water from an underground aquifer that had been under a decree that restricted how much water could be removed since 2005. Just weeks before the project was rubber-stamped by the environmental authority, that decree had been upgraded to a complete prohibition on new extraction.

The water use estimates set off alarm bells for the residents. Chile had already been in an unprecedented drought since 2010. By 2021, more than half the country’s 19 million residents lived in areas experiencing severe water scarcity, forcing hundreds of rural communities to rely on tankers to deliver drinking water.

The local activists ultimately built the case against one of the largest companies on the planet. After months of meetings and advocacy to spread awareness, they were able to put a referendum question to the residents of Cerrillos about the project in December 2019. The results were damning: 49% of voters chose to reject the project, while 38% wanted it to go forward.

After both the municipality and community members filed claims against Google in 2020, the company returned with a new proposal in February 2022. It offered to cool the data center exclusively with air-conditioning rather than with water.

Across the city in Quilicura, opposition was building too. Microsoft announced its intention to build a data center in the community in 2022, the same year strict water-rationing rules had come into effect in Santiago. As in Cerrillos, residents were worried that another large data center would threaten their access to water and provide little in return.

Vicente Bardales, a member of the Quilicura Socio Environmental Resistance group, told Rest of World that the compa

analysis.tldr: Big tech's massive water consumption for AI could trigger tighter global regulations and higher costs, potentially influencing how data centers are built and operated in countries like India.
the_story: Training early versions of ChatGPT required 185,000 gallons of water, and everyday interactions consume significant amounts.
A single large data center can consume between 1 and 5 million gallons of water daily, rivaling the usage of a small city.
Specialized chips called GPUs (graphics processing units) used for AI run much hotter, requiring extensive water or energy for cooling.
In Chile, local residents organized resistance against a planned Google data center in Cerrillos that threatened to consume massive amounts of local drinking water during a severe drought.
Faced with local pushback and legal challenges, Google eventually revised its proposal to cool the data center with air-conditioning instead of water.
analysis.what_happened: Tech companies are building massive data centers to power artificial intelligence (AI), but these facilities generate immense heat and require millions of gallons of clean water daily to stay cool. Because data centers prefer cheap and accessible public drinking water over costly treatment plants, their heavy usage is sparking protests and community pushback in water-stressed regions around the world.
analysis.analogy: It is like a giant factory moving into a small village during a severe drought and using up all the water from the local well just to keep its heavy machinery from overheating.
why_it_matters_india: Global tech giants facing pushback abroad may shift or expand their massive data center investments to different regions.
India is also seeing a boom in data center construction driven by cloud computing and AI demand.
Local communities and regulators in water-stressed parts of India may scrutinize upcoming data center projects much more closely.
Stricter environmental rules could increase operational costs for technology infrastructure projects in India.

impacts.rationale: Higher global scrutiny and rules on AI infrastructure could slightly delay tech spending, affecting big IT service providers — mildly negative for investors.

watch_next: Whether other countries introduce strict local water-usage rules for tech companies
How Indian authorities and local communities respond to new data center proposals in water-scarce regions
analysis.caveats: The article text cuts off near the end, but the core reporting focuses entirely on events in Chile and general global data center water challenges.

history.title: The cure that caused a recession on purpose
history.what: Paul Volcker, newly in charge of the US Federal Reserve, raised interest rates to nearly 20% to break an inflation that had run for a decade. He knew it would cause a severe recession. He did it anyway.
history.why: Through the 1970s the Fed had repeatedly raised rates, seen unemployment rise, lost its nerve and cut again. Each cycle ended with inflation higher than before. Americans had stopped believing inflation would ever be controlled, so they demanded bigger pay rises and firms raised prices pre-emptively — which made the inflation self-fulfilling. The problem was no longer economic; it was that nobody believed the promise.
history.impact: Unemployment reached nearly 11%, the worst since the Depression. Farm foreclosures and factory closures spread across the American Midwest. But inflation fell from about 14% to under 3%. The bond market, which had been a graveyard for a decade, began a bull run that lasted forty years — and shares followed it.
history.policy: The policy was simply to keep rates punishingly high until expectations broke, and to say so publicly and repeatedly. What it established was the doctrine that a central bank's credibility is its most valuable asset, and is worth a recession to protect.
history.consequence: Every inflation-fighting central bank since has followed the same script, including India's RBI and every bank that raised rates sharply in 2022. The forty-year fall in interest rates that followed also inflated the price of nearly every asset on earth — shares, bonds, property — which is a large part of why the generation that invested after 1982 did so well, and why repeating their returns from today's starting point is harder.
history.pattern: Inflation is beaten by breaking what people expect, not by any single rate decision. That is why central bankers sound repetitive and stern: the words are the policy. When a central bank starts caring more about growth than about its own credibility, the inflation problem is about to get longer.
history.india_echo: The RBI made the same choice in 2013-14 under Raghuram Rajan, raising rates into a slowdown to defend the rupee and break inflation, and then adopting a formal inflation target in 2016. India's inflation has been far better behaved since — the policy worked, and the mechanism was credibility.
history.watch_for: Central bankers talking about expectations becoming "unanchored". That is the technical phrase for the 1970s problem, and it signals they are prepared to tolerate real pain.
